title: 201 Great Ideas for Your Small Business (3rd Edition)
author: Jane Applegate (Bloomberg Press)
summary:
201 Great Ideas for Your Small Business, now in its third edition from Bloomberg Press, is a practical reference guide by longtime small-business journalist and consultant Jane Applegate. Like Jeremy Kourdi's similarly structured 100 Great Business Ideas, the book presents its content as a large number of discrete, numbered ideas — 201 of them — organized into topic-based chapters covering the full life cycle of running a small business, from setting up an office and managing client relationships through marketing, international expansion, and crisis management.

Applegate draws each idea from real small-business owners she interviewed over years of reporting and consulting work, giving the book a grounded, anecdotal quality distinct from more theory-driven business texts. The third edition, updated substantially from earlier versions, places particular emphasis on online marketing, social media, and navigating difficult economic conditions, reflecting the book's ongoing revision to stay current with how small businesses actually operate.

A distinctive feature of this edition is its closing chapter, "Great Ideas and Insights from VIPs," which departs from the numbered-idea format to present short interview-style profiles of well-known businesspeople and entrepreneurs — including Michael Bloomberg, Tom Peters, Guy Kawasaki, Kay Koplovitz, Wally Amos, and Lillian Vernon — each distilled into a single "top tip" framing (for example, "Herb Kelleher: Be a Maverick" or "Tom Peters: Forget Credentials"). This closing chapter functions as a capstone that reframes the book's practical, day-to-day advice within the broader career philosophies of recognizable business figures.

Throughout the body chapters, Applegate covers a wide practical range: everyday operational efficiencies (like orienting new offices for natural light to cut costs), building informal advisory boards, streamlining meetings, navigating international expansion (including chapters on exporting, manufacturing abroad, and country-specific guidance for markets like Mexico, India, China, and Russia), and marketing in a social-media-driven environment. The tone throughout is accessible and anecdote-driven rather than academic, consistent with the book's origin in Applegate's journalism and small-business consulting work rather than formal management research.

Because the book explicitly organizes its 201 ideas into numbered chapters by topic (unlike Kourdi's unordered format), this entry follows the book's own broad topical groupings as best confirmed through available tables of contents, while noting that full chapter-by-chapter titles for the entire book could not be independently confirmed beyond the sections referenced in available excerpts.

sections.title: Running Day-to-Day Operations
sections.summary:
This chapter cluster covers the practical mechanics of operating a small business, including setting up efficient office space, forming informal advisory boards to get outside perspective on tough decisions, and streamlining meetings to protect limited time. Applegate draws these ideas directly from small-business owners she has interviewed, giving practical, low-cost fixes rather than abstract operational theory.

The section emphasizes resourcefulness — several ideas explicitly target businesses without large budgets, such as designing new office space to maximize natural light and reduce utility costs, or building an informal (rather than costly, formal) advisory structure.

It sets up the book's later marketing-focused chapters by establishing that operational discipline is treated as a prerequisite for effective growth, not a separate concern from it.
keyLessons: Look for low-cost operational fixes (like natural lighting or space layout) that reduce ongoing costs.
Build an informal advisory board of trusted outside perspectives rather than assuming you need a formal, costly one.
Protect limited time by deliberately streamlining recurring meetings.

sections.title: Marketing and Client Relationships
sections.summary:
This cluster addresses how small businesses find, meet, and retain clients, including practical guidance on where to meet clients without a dedicated office space and how to woo prospective clients effectively. The third edition substantially expands this area to address online marketing and social media, reflecting how small-business client acquisition had shifted since earlier editions.

The section draws heavily on real small-business owner interviews rather than abstract marketing theory, giving the ideas a practical, replicable quality suited to businesses with limited marketing budgets.

It leads into the book's chapters on economic resilience by connecting strong client relationships to a business's ability to weather difficult periods.
keyLessons: Find creative, low-cost ways to meet and impress clients even without a traditional office space.
Update your marketing approach to include online and social channels rather than relying solely on traditional methods.
Treat client relationship quality as a factor in your business's resilience during downturns, not just its growth.

sections.title: International Business
sections.summary:
This chapter cluster addresses small businesses looking to expand internationally, covering topics such as exporting products, moving manufacturing to Mexico, forging international alliances, and country-specific guidance for doing business in India, Russia, and China. It also addresses practical compliance topics like meeting U.S. safety rules for products made abroad and translating marketing materials appropriately.

The section treats international expansion as accessible to small businesses, not just large corporations, while being explicit about the additional compliance, cultural, and communication work required to do it well.

It closes by connecting international ambition back to the book's broader theme of resourcefulness — treating global expansion as one more growth lever available to a well-run small business rather than an exclusively large-company strategy.
keyLessons: Research country-specific business norms and etiquette before attempting international expansion.
Confirm compliance requirements (like U.S. safety rules for goods made abroad) before finalizing overseas manufacturing.
Properly translate and adapt marketing materials for each new international market rather than exporting your domestic materials unchanged.

sections.title: Great Ideas and Insights from VIPs
sections.summary:
The book's closing chapter departs from the numbered-idea format to present short, interview-derived profiles of well-known entrepreneurs and businesspeople, each condensed into a single defining "top tip" — for example, Herb Kelleher framed around being a maverick, Tom Peters framed around disregarding credentials, and Lillian Vernon framed around mail-order retail expertise.

This chapter functions as a capstone, reframing the book's granular, day-to-day advice within the broader career philosophies of recognizable figures, giving readers a higher-level, more aspirational close to an otherwise highly tactical book.

The book ends without a traditional summary conclusion, closing instead on these individual profiles, consistent with its identity as a practical reference collection rather than a single unified argument.
keyLessons: Distill your own guiding business philosophy into a single, memorable principle, the way each VIP profile does.
Look to varied, even contradictory, role models (a maverick versus a credentialist skeptic) rather than a single template for success.
Treat well-known entrepreneurs' philosophies as inspiration to adapt, not scripts to copy directly.
Look for low-cost, practical operational fixes rather than assuming growth requires large capital investment.
Build an informal outside advisory perspective into your decision-making, even without a formal board.
Protect limited time by deliberately streamlining recurring meetings and processes.
Update your marketing approach to include online and social channels, not just traditional methods.
Treat strong client relationships as part of your business's resilience during difficult economic periods.
Research country-specific norms and compliance requirements before pursuing international expansion.
Adapt (not just translate) your marketing materials for each new market you enter.
Distill your own guiding business philosophy into one clear, memorable principle.

quotes.text: It doesn't matter whether you're running a fast-growing factory or a cozy suburban beauty salon—I have great ideas for you.
quotes.attribution: Jane Applegate, 201 Great Ideas for Your Small Business
quotes.category: On the Purpose of the Book

quotes.text: Think of this book as the Physician's Desk Reference of small business. You may not use all 201 ideas at once, but over the course of building your business, you'll probably need many of them.
quotes.attribution: jacket endorsement quoted in promotional material for 201 Great Ideas for Your Small Business

conceptsFrameworks.name: Numbered Idea Format
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The book's core structural device: 201 discrete, individually numbered practical ideas, each addressing a specific small-business problem, organized into topical chapters so readers can locate advice relevant to their immediate situation rather than reading sequentially.

conceptsFrameworks.name: VIP "Top Tip" Profiles
conceptsFrameworks.definition: The closing chapter's format, condensing each interviewed businessperson's philosophy into a single defining principle (e.g., "Be a Maverick," "Forget Credentials"), used as a capstone device to connect the book's tactical advice to broader, more aspirational business thinking.
conceptsFrameworks.sourceSection: Great Ideas and Insights from VIPs

actionSteps: Audit your current office or workspace setup for one low-cost change (lighting, layout, or logistics) that could reduce ongoing operating costs.
Assemble an informal group of three to five trusted outside contacts you can consult before major business decisions.
Update one piece of your marketing materials or approach to better reflect current online and social-media norms.
If considering international expansion, research the specific compliance and cultural requirements for one target country before taking any other step.
reflectionQuestions: Where in your business are you assuming a solution requires significant capital, when a low-cost operational fix might work just as well?
Who would you add to an informal advisory circle, and what blind spot would they help you see?
If you had to distill your own business philosophy into a single memorable principle, the way the book's VIP profiles do, what would it be?

points: As with Kourdi's similarly structured book, the sheer number of discrete ideas (201) makes it difficult to prioritize which advice matters most for a specific business's stage or industry; the book offers limited guidance on sequencing or trade-offs between competing ideas.

Because the book has gone through multiple editions with substantial revisions (the publisher notes 174 of 201 ideas changed to varying degrees between the second and third editions), older copies or excerpts in circulation may reflect meaningfully outdated advice, particularly around online marketing, which changes faster than most other business practices covered.

The closing VIP chapter's single-tip framing of well-known businesspeople (e.g., reducing Tom Peters's philosophy to "forget credentials") is necessarily reductive and risks oversimplifying more nuanced perspectives from figures with substantial independent bodies of work.

The book's anecdote-driven, interview-based approach means its evidentiary basis is largely qualitative and self-reported by the small-business owners interviewed, rather than independently verified outcome data.
criticalTake.contextNote: The publisher's own promotional materials for the third edition acknowledge the online-marketing and social-media sections were the most substantially rewritten from earlier editions, suggesting the earlier editions' marketing advice specifically should be treated as more dated than the book's operational and international-business content.

whoThisIsFor: Small-business owners looking for a browsable, anecdote-rich reference of practical fixes across operations, marketing, and international expansion, rather than a single strategic framework.
whenToReadThis: Best used as an ongoing reference to consult when facing a specific operational or marketing problem, revisited periodically as your business grows into new challenges (like international expansion).

authorBio.name: Jane Applegate
authorBio.bio:
Jane Applegate is a small-business journalist, author, and consultant whose work has focused on translating real small-business owners' experiences into practical, replicable advice. She built much of the book's content through years of interviewing entrepreneurs across a wide range of industries and business sizes.

Her connection to Bloomberg, including a direct working relationship with Michael Bloomberg (acknowledged in the book itself), reflects her positioning within a broader ecosystem of Bloomberg-branded small-business media, including 201greatideas.com and related video content produced alongside the book.

sourceNotes:
Synthesis is based on web-search verification of the book's chapter-numbered idea structure, third-edition revision history (174 of 201 ideas revised or updated), and the confirmed closing "Great Ideas and Insights from VIPs" chapter with its named contributors and single-tip framings. Full chapter-by-chapter titles across the entire book's topical organization could not be independently confirmed beyond the sections referenced in available excerpts, so this entry's section breakdown reflects the topical clusters that could be verified rather than a complete internal table of contents.
